ADAPT: On the International Day of Persons with Disabilities, we’re proud to highlight the Straz Strong Foundation, created by Humboldt Broncos crash survivor Ryan Straschnitzki. Straz Strong helps people adapt by supporting access to adaptive sports, technologies, and opportunities that promote independence and inclusion. Their work showcases the strength of communities that come together to break barriers and champion resilience across Canada.
AGATE: Canada is home to stunning agates, including the famous Thunder Bay Agate, known for its deep red and orange hues from iron oxidation! These colourful nodules form in volcanic rock and can be found along Lake Superior's north shore, as well as in British Columbia, Alberta, and the Maritimes. Rockhounds love hunting for these hidden gems - finding an agate is like holding a piece of Earth's history in your hand!
AHEAD: "Ahead by a Century" is a song by Canadian rock band The Tragically Hip. It was released as the lead single from the band's fifth studio album, Trouble at the Henhouse. The song reached #1 on Canada's singles chart, and is the band's most successful single in their native Canada. The song was certified platinum in Canada in 2016, and it was the last song performed by the band at their final concert on August 20, 2016.
ALBUM: The Juno Award for Album of the Year is an annual award presented by the Canadian Academy of Recording Arts and Sciences for the best album released in Canada. It has been awarded since 1975. Arcade Fire, Celine Dion, Michael Bublé and The Weeknd are the artists with the most wins in this category with three each; Dion is the most nominated artist with 12 nominations.
ALONE: The mission of No Stone Left Alone is to honour the sacrifice and service of Canada’s military by educating students and placing poppies on the headstones of veterans every November. No Stone Left Alone was officially launched in 2011 to help ensure an enduring national respect and gratitude for the sacrifice of the Canadian men and women who have lost their lives in the service of peace, at home and abroad. It has become the mission of founder Maureen Bianchini Purvis to see that one day all of the soldiers' headstones would have a poppy placed in their honour, with truly No Stone Left Alone. You can donate to the No Stone Left Alone Memorial Foundation at nostoneleftalone.ca/donate.
ALTAR: Canada has several famous altars, mostly found in its historic churches and cathedrals. These altars are known not just for their religious significance but also for their architectural and artistic beauty. A few notable examples include the altars at Notre-Dame Basilica and Basilica of Saint Joseph's Oratory in Montreal, and the St. Michael's Cathedral Basilica altar in Toronto. These altars not only serve as the focal points for worship but also stand as significant artistic and architectural landmarks in Canada's religious and cultural landscape.
ATLAS: The Armstrong Whitworth Atlas was a British single-engine two-seat biplane. It served as an army co-operation aircraft for the Royal Canadian Air Force in the 1920s and 1930s. April 1, 2024 marked 100 years of service for the Royal Canadian Air Force as a distinct military element. The RCAF Centennial is an opportunity to showcase Air Force personnel and their accomplishments, demonstrate air and space power, enhance the reputation of the RCAF, and proudly honour its distinguished history and heritage.
AUGER: Ice fishing is a popular winter pastime in Canada that is enjoyed on many Canadian lakes! Small holes are drilled through the frozen lake surfaces using ice augers, allowing for the fun activity of fishing during the winter months! Billed as the "Ice Fishing Capital of Canada," more people fish on Lake Simcoe, Ontario in winter than all other seasons combined.
AWARD: The 2023 Juno Awards took place in Edmonton, Alberta last night! The annual awards ceremony celebrates outstanding achievements in Canadian music. The Juno Awards began in 1964 as the RPM Gold Leaf Awards, and in 1971 they were renamed the Juno Awards after the Roman goddess and in tribute to Pierre Juneau, the first chairperson of the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC) who was responsible for introducing the Canadian content quota to Canadian radio that year.
AXIOM: An axiom is a basic rule accepted as true without needing proof, and it’s where all logical thinking begins. World Logic Day on January 14 celebrates these foundational ideas, the same way games like Canuckle and Canoku start with simple rules that guide every word guess and emoji placement. From letters to patterns, great puzzles are built one solid axiom at a time.
AZURE: The word azure means bright sky-blue, a colour seen across Canada’s vast skies and lakes. In heraldry, azure also appears in The Coat of Arms of Canada on the shield, representing the royal emblems of Ireland (a harp) and France (three fleurs-de-lis). Together with symbols from England and Scotland, these elements reflect the historical nations that shaped Canada’s founding.
BADGE: On Canadian Armed Forces Day (celebrated on the first Sunday in June), we recognize the dedication and service of Canada's military personnel. In the Canadian Armed Forces, a badge carries deep meaning - reflecting a unit's identity, honouring its history, and building pride among those who wear it. From regimental crests to specialized qualification badges, each one tells a story of dedication and service to Canada. Many incorporate iconic symbols like maple leaves, beavers, or crowns, proudly connecting each badge to Canada's heritage.
BAGEL: The Montréal bagel is one of Canada's most iconic and coveted snacks. It is a distinctive variety of handmade bagel that traditionally has a prounounced sweet taste and a chewy and dense texture, and is always baked in a wood-fired oven. The bagel first arrived in Montréal with the wave of Jewish immigrants from Eastern Europe in the early 1900s.
BALSA: Balsa wood is lightweight yet incredibly strong, making it a go-to material for Canadian crafters and hobbyists! Native to South America, balsa is used in model airplanes, ping pong paddles, and even surfboards. Many Canadian builders appreciate its ease of use and buoyancy, making it perfect for crafting floatable objects. So next time you spot a model plane or a small raft in Canada, there's a good chance balsa wood is behind the design!
BANDS: Today is National Indigenous Veterans Day, a time to honour the First Nations, Inuit, and Métis peoples who have served in uniform. Thousands of Indigenous veterans from communities and bands across Canada volunteered in both World Wars, Korea, and beyond – often travelling far from home to defend a country that did not yet grant them full rights. Their courage, resilience, and leadership are now formally recognized and remembered each November 8, as Canadians pay tribute to the vital role Indigenous veterans have played in our shared history.
BANJO: The Banjo Bowl is the annual rematch game between the Winnipeg Blue Bombers and Saskatchewan Roughriders of the Canadian Football League after the Labour Day Classic. The game has been sold out every year since 2005. As of the 2023 season, Winnipeg leads the series 12–7. The Blue Bombers will host the CFL's Western Final this Saturday, after the team secured the top spot in the division for the third season in a row.
BASIN: Canada is home to numerous basins, including Canada Basin in the Arctic, Basin Head Beach in Prince Edward Island, the Sudbury Basin in Ontario, and the Western Canada Sedimentary Basin which underlies 1.4 million square kilometres across Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, and British Columbia.
BATHE: From coast to coast, Canadians have long sought out steamy, mineral-rich waters to bathe in and unwind. At Liard River Hot Springs in northern BC, you can soak beneath a canopy of boreal forest. In the Rockies, Radium and Banff Upper Hot Springs offer stunning alpine views. Even the Yukon boasts Takhini Hot Springs, where bathers compete in a frozen hairdo contest each winter! Wherever you roam, there's a hot spring waiting to to help you relax - Canada's natural spa experience.
BATIK: Batik is a centuries-old textile art that uses wax and dye to create beautiful, layered designs. While it originated in Indonesia, batik has found a vibrant home in Canada, where artists have embraced the technique to reflect uniquely Canadian themes – like northern lights, maple leaves, and coastal landscapes. From community workshops to gallery exhibitions, Canadian batik artists continue to blend global tradition with local creativity in bold, colourful ways.
BEARD: In Canada, springtime means one thing for hockey fans: the return of the playoff beard! This legendary tradition sees players (and even some fans!) grow out their facial hair as long as their team stays in the playoffs. It's believed to have started with the New York Islanders in the 1980s, but it's become a true staple of Canadian hockey culture. From scruffy stubble to full-on lumberjack, a playoff beard is more than just facial hair - it's a symbol of hope, grit, and superstition on the road to the Cup!
BEECH: The American Beech tree is a common sight in the forests of eastern Canada and in Ontario and Quebec. Known for its smooth, grey bark and vibrant fall colours, this tree can live for more than 300 years! Beech trees play an important role in Canadian ecosystems, providing food for wildlife such as squirrels, birds, and even black bears, who enjoy feasting on its nuts. Whether you're hiking through a forest or simply admiring their beauty, beech trees are a quiet giant in Canada's natural landscape!
BELLY: In the heart of St. John's, Newfoundland, YellowBelly Brewery serves up more than just great beer - it pours out history! Housed in one of the city's oldest buildings, this brewery gets its name from the 'Yellowbellies,' a term historically tied to Irish immigrants and their role in the Irish Rebellion of 1798. The building itself dates back to the early 1800s and even survived the devastating Great Fire of 1892. Today, visitors can enjoy a pint while soaking in the rich past of this legendary spot - where history and hops go hand in hand!
BELTS: Wampum are tubular purple and white beads made from shells. Wampum are used primarily by Indigenous peoples of the Eastern Woodlands for ornamental, ceremonial, diplomatic and commercial purposes. Belts made of wampum were used to mark agreements between peoples. Wampum belts and other wampum bead artifacts continue to hold significance for Indigenous peoples and any treaties or agreements they might represent.
BENCH: In the House of Commons, MPs with leadership roles sit on the front bench, while everyone else sits on the back bench. Backbenchers may not wear the cabinet title, but they’re far from idle, reviewing legislation in committees, introducing private members’ bills, and taking part in Question Period. In the 45th Canadian Parliament, all 343 MPs, including the backbench, keep the work of democracy moving every day.
BERRY: It's berry season in Canada! The start of summer means an abundance of fresh strawberries, raspberries, blueberries, blackberries and Saskatoon berries. The Saskatoon berry shrub is native to western Canada and has been an important food source for those inhabiting this landscape for thousands of years. In fact, the name Saskatoon is derived from the Cree word ‘Mis-sask-quah-too-mina’ for the berry producing plant.
BINGO: The game of Bingo has been a beloved pastime in Canada for decades! In fact, the first official Canadian Bingo hall opened in the 1940s in British Columbia, and the game quickly became a popular way to raise money for charities, schools, and local communities. Whether played at a community centre or as a family game night favourite, Bingo remains a fun way to bring Canadians together! From coast to coast, Canadians have enjoyed shouting "Bingo!" as a way to win big and support their communities at the same time.
BIRTH: Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island has the distinction of being the Birthplace of Canadian Confederation. It was in Charlottetown in September 1864, where delegates from Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and the Canadas met to discuss what was originally meant to be Maritime Union but soon became a union of British North America. They were united into one federation called the Dominion of Canada, on July 1, 1867.
BLADE: Today marks the start of the Western Hockey League (WHL) regular season in Canada! The Saskatoon Blades are a Canadian major junior ice hockey team based in Saskatoon, Saskatchewan. Founded in 1964, the Blades were a charter team of the then-Western Canada Junior Hockey League in 1966, and are the only club that has played every season in the league in its original location. The team has twice hosted the Memorial Cup tournament, in 1989 and in 2013.
BLAME: "Blame Canada" is a satirical song from the 1999 animated film South Park: Bigger, Longer & Uncut, written by Trey Parker and Marc Shaiman. The song was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Original Song at the 72nd Academy Awards. "Blame Canada" has become a catch phrase for shifting attention away from a problem or serious social issue by humorously laying responsibility on Canada.
BLIND: In response to rising blindness rates caused by the Halifax explosion and veterans returning home from World War I, the Canadian National Institute for the Blind (CNIB) was founded and incorporated by a group of seven Canadian men - several veterans and blind men among them. Since the founding in 1918, the CNIB Foundation has been creating programs, providing services and advocating to change the lives of Canadians who are blind or partially sighted. CNIB is a non-profit organization driven to change what it is to be blind today.
BLING: Hotline Bling by Canadian artist Drake became one of the defining hits of 2015, reaching No. 2 on the Billboard Hot 100 and dominating charts around the world. Known for its minimalist production and instantly recognizable music video, the track spent weeks in the top tier of the charts and earned multiple Grammy wins, further cementing Drake’s global influence as a Canadian music powerhouse.
BOGEY: In golf, a bogey means one stroke over par. In Canada, Triple Bogey Brewing Company embraces the game’s spirit with golf-inspired drinks. Founded in 2014 by Geoff and Megan Tait, the brewery offers premium lagers and ready-to-drink cocktails like Transfusions, Water Hazard, and Azalea. Their products are available at over 400 golf courses and 1,000 locations across Canada, bringing a taste of golf culture to golf fans nationwide.
BOOTH: Speakers Corner began in 1990 with a video booth outside the Citytv studios in Toronto. The booth's original intent was for viewers to record news commentary and "letter to the editor" segments for broadcast on CityPulse, but the booth soon proved so popular that the decision was soon made to create a full half-hour weekly series. The show was an example of Citytv founder Moses Znaimer's philosophy of interactive broadcasting, and essentially created what some 21st-century media outlets would retroactively label as a precursor to YouTube.
BOOZE: Canada is known for its thriving alcohol industry, producing a wide variety of spirits, wines, and beers enjoyed by people around the world. From award-winning whiskies to crisp ice wines harvested in the vineyards of Ontario's Niagara region, Canada offers a diverse and flavourful selection of alcoholic beverages. Whether you're enjoying a glass of Canadian wine or enjoying a cold craft beer from one of Canada's many breweries, the alcohol industry in Canada is sure to quench your thirst and leave you wanting more!
BOXES: Boxing Day in Canada has a unique blend of traditions! While it originally involved giving “Christmas boxes” to workers and those in need, today, Canadians also embrace it as a day for major shopping sales and hockey. From filling donation boxes for local charities to watching Team Canada in the World Juniors, Boxing Day is all about generosity and community spirit - true Canadian values!
BRASS: The Royal Canadian Mounted Police, or Mounties, are known for their distinctive brass-buttoned uniforms and their role as national symbols of Canada. Mounties also wear a brass shoulder title pin on the epaulettes of their uniform. Canadian Brass is a brass quintent formed in 1970 in Toronto that was named "one of the most popular brass ensembles in the world". They were the first brass quintet to play on the main stage at Carnegie Hall in New York, and they also appeared on The Tonight Show with Johnny Carson.
BRICK: The largest ever LEGO brick flag was built in honour of Canada Day 2018 at LEGOLAND Discovery Centre Toronto in Vaughan, Ontario. The Guinness World Record holding flag displays the maple leaf and measures 3.47 m (11 ft 7 in) tall and 6.46 m (21 ft 2 in) wide. It’s made up of a whopping 248,062 tiny bricks and weighs 1,110 lb (500 kg). Led by Canada’s only master model builder, Noel Straatsma, the record title utilized the talents of 10 builders, and required four days of construction.
BRINE: Brine isn’t just salty water – it’s the starting point for one of Canada’s biggest salt success stories. At its Goderich operation on Lake Huron, Sifto Canada operates the world’s largest rock salt mine, producing millions of tonnes of bulk salt each year. A separate nearby facility pumps up underground brine, then evaporates and refines it into around 95,000 tonnes high-purity, food-grade salt each year. From seasoning kitchens to preserving food across the country, Canadian brine plays a quietly essential role at the table.
BROOK: Canada is home to countless brooks that meander through lush forests and rugged landscapes. These babbling waterways provide essential habitats for fish like brook trout, a prized catch for anglers in Canadian waters. Whether you're hiking in Algonquin Park or fishing in Newfoundland's rivers, encountering a brook is a tranquil reminder of Canada's pristine natural beauty. So, next time you wander through Canada's wilderness, listen closely - the whispers of a brook might just lead you to an unforgettable adventure!
BROOM: The original corn brooms are a part of curling history in Canada. Prior to the 1950s, most curling brooms were made of corn strands and were similar to household brooms of the day. In 1958, Fern Marchessault of Montreal inverted the corn straw in the centre of the broom, improving the speed and force of the broom striking the ice. This style of corn broom was referred to as the Blackjack. Today, brushes have replaced traditional corn brooms at every level of curling.
BUGGY: Mennonite groups can be found across Canada, with over half of the population residing in urban areas such as Winnipeg, Vancouver, and Kitchener-Waterloo. Almost 200,000 Mennonites call Canada home. Waterloo Region is home to the largest population of Old Order Mennonites in Canada, particularly in the areas around St. Jacobs and Elmira. They are often seen on the local roads using their traditional horse and buggy transportation, and many also use horses to pull the implements in their farm fields.
BULLY: Pink Shirt Day is an annual event against bullying held in Canada on the last Wednesday of February. Participants wear pink shirts and attend or host informative events to raise awareness about bullying, particularly in schools. Also known as Anti-Bullying Day, the initiative was started in Canada in 2007 by two teenagers from Berwick, Nova Scotia when a fellow Grade 9 student was being teased and bullied for wearing a pink shirt on the first day of school.
BYLAW: From coast to coast, Canada is home to some wonderfully strange and amusing bylaws that reflect the quirks and character of its communities. In Dawson City, Yukon, it's illegal to disturb a moose, including honking at one! In Calgary, Alberta, you're not allowed to put your feet on benches, planters, or sculptures in public spaces. And In Souris, Prince Edward Island, you can't build a snowman taller than 30 inches on a corner lot – safety first, even for frosty friends! These odd rules show how unique (and Canadian!) our local bylaws can be.
CABIN: Cabin is another name for a cottage, and Canada has no shortage of weekend getaway spots!
CACTI: Four species of cacti are native to Canada: pincushion cactus, little prickly pear cactus, common plains prickly pear cactus, and eastern prickly pear cactus. All of these species are at the northern limits of their distribution. In 1985, the Committee on the Status of Endangered Wildlife in Canada officially designated the cactus as an endangered plant.
CADET: In the Canadian Armed Forces, the appointment of officer cadet is held by beginning officers, as well as students attending the Royal Military College of Canada in Kingston, Ontario and the Collège militaire royal de Saint-Jean in Saint-Jean-sur-Richelieu, Québec. Officer cadets and naval cadets complete the Regular Officer Training Plan to become commissioned officers in the Canadian Armed Forces.
CAMEL: The Sopwith Camel became the most successful British fighter of the First World War. Several Canadian aces used the Camel as their mount. Very manoeuvrable, it could be tricky to fly in the hands of a novice pilot. For experienced pilots, however, the aircraft proved to be a superb fighter. The guns were mounted on the forward fuselage with their breeches enclosed in a faired metal cowling - a "hump" that gave the Camel its name.
CANOE: In Canada, the canoe has long been associated with the fur trade and the romantic figure of the voyageur.
CARAT: Happy Mother's Day from Canuckle! Canadian mines produced 18.6 million carats of rough diamonds valued at $2.25 billion in 2019, making Canada the world's third largest producer of rough diamonds by value.
CARDS: Kelvington, Saskatchewan is known as "Canada's Hockey Factory"! A giant hockey cards monument was built to celebrate Kelvington's famous hockey players, including Lloyd Gronsdahl, Barry Melrose, Joe Kocur, Wendel Clark, Kerry Clark, and Kory Kocur.
CARGO: Did you know that Canada is home to one of the world's largest cargo ports? The Port of Vancouver, located in British Columbia, is not only Canada's largest port but also the third-largest port in North America by total tonnage. Serving as a vital gateway for trade between North America and Asia, the Port of Vancouver handles a diverse range of cargo, including containerized goods, bulk commodities, automobiles, and more. With state-of-the-art facilities and strategic transportation networks, the port plays a crucial role in supporting Canada's economy and global trade.
CATCH: Prince Edward Island offers anglers the chance to catch one of the world's mightiest big-game fish - the bluefin tuna! The first bluefin landed on P.E.I. was out of North Lake Harbour in 1967. By 1970s the catch rates had increased and a charter business began on the island. North Lake soon became known as one of the few places you could catch a fish weighing over 1000 pounds and was coined the "Tuna Capital of the World" because of all the world record catches.
CENTS: Street Cents is a newsmagazine TV series directed at teenagers that originally aired on CBC Television between 1989 and 2006. Street Cents focused on consumer and media awareness for young people. The show has won several Gemini Awards and even an International Emmy for Best Youth Programming or Series, and was lauded by critics for its efforts to be inclusive and representative of Canada's youth. Jonathan Torrens was one of the original hosts of the show. Street Cents returned in a new format in 2022, led by a group of dynamic content creators. Targeted to teens, the new version of the beloved youth brand has launched on TikTok with a focus on making financial literacy useful, relatable and entertaining through daily short form video content.
CHAIN: Did you know that a group of lynx is called a "chain"? The Canada lynx, a native species to Canada, is known for its distinctive tufted ears and large, padded paws that act like snowshoes in the winter. These elusive cats are most commonly found in the boreal forests of Canada, where they primarily hunt snowshoe hares. While lynx are typically solitary animals, the term "chain" is used to describe a group of them when they do come together. Seeing a chain of lynx in the wild is a rare and remarkable sight, reflecting the rich biodiversity of Canada's wilderness.
CHAMP: The War Amps has been supporting amputees across Canada for over a century! Their CHAMP (Child Amputee) Program, founded in 1975, helps young amputees by providing financial aid for artificial limbs, peer support, and empowering opportunities. CHAMP helps kids build confidence and independence, ensuring they can thrive. You might also recognize the War Amps' iconic key tag service, which has been helping Canadians reunite with lost keys since 1946! You can donate to The War Amps today and help provide life-changing support to amputees in Canada.
CHANT: Today is National Indigenous Peoples Day! On June 21, we recognize and celebrate the history, heritage, resilience and diversity of First Nations, Inuit and Métis across Canada. Chants play a vital role in Indigenous culture in Canada, used in ceremonies, healing, and storytelling for generations. These rhythmic vocalizations help preserve history, connect communities, and honour ancestors. Chants, alongside traditional songs, are a way for Indigenous peoples to maintain their cultural identity and pass knowledge from one generation to the next. They are a powerful form of expression and resilience within Canada’s rich cultural mosaic.
CHESS: Medicine Hat, Alberta is home to the world's largest chess board! The chess set measures 5.89 metres on each side and the king pieces stand almost 4 feet tall. The board was entered in the record books in 2009, four years after its completion by the Medicine Hat Chess Club. You can find the chess set in a courtyard outside the Medicine Hat Public Library in the summer months.
CHEST: Our chest rises and falls with every breath - something we often take for granted. Respiratory therapists across Canada are the experts who help keep those breaths strong and steady. Represented by the Canadian Society of Respiratory Therapists (CSRT), they care for people with conditions affecting the lungs and chest in hospitals, communities, and beyond. This week from October 19-25, the CSRT celebrates Respiratory Therapy Week, honouring the dedication and vital work of Canada’s respiratory therapists!
CHURN: Operating a wooden barrel churn was a demanding daily task in many pioneer households across Canada. Often done by children, the process involved steadily agitating fresh cream for long periods until the butterfat separated from the liquid buttermilk. Though labour-intensive, churning butter provided an important source of fat and nutrition in early Canadian life.
CLASS: On October 5th, we celebrated World Teachers' Day, a day to recognize the incredible role teachers play in shaping the minds of the next generation across the country! Canada is home to over 500,000 teachers who bring passion and dedication to the classroom each day. In fact, Canada is known for its strong public education system, consistently ranking among the best in the world. Whether they're in small rural schools or bustling urban centres, teachers in Canada ensure students have access to quality education from coast to coast.
CLERK: The Clerk of the Privy Council is the professional head of the Public Service of Canada. As the deputy minister for the Privy Council Office (the Prime Minister's department), the clerk is the senior civil servant in the Government of Canada and serves as the secretary to the Cabinet.
CLIFF: Baffin Island, Canada is home to Mount Thor, the world's tallest vertical cliff. In fact, it's steeper than vertical, with a 105-degree overhang. Check out this article by Jeopardy champ Ken Jennings all about Mount Thor!
COACH: Henry Ruttan was a prominent businessman, inventor, and politician in Upper Canada who revolutionized railway travel. In 1858, he patented an innovative system for heating and cooling railway coaches, which was adopted by several railway companies across North America. His system used the motion of the train to force outside air through ducts and a wash tank, where the air was cleaned, humidified, and cooled. During winter, the system was adapted to heat the air entering the cars, making train travel more comfortable year-round. Ruttan’s invention was a game-changer for passenger comfort and a brilliant example of Canadian ingenuity!
COBRA: There are plenty of animals that are considered to be icons in Canada including beavers, moose and polar bears. However, anyone who lives in the Great White North knows that Canada geese are the country's true mascots, despite their notoriously bad attitude. They hiss, they honk, and worst of all, they chase you down if you get too close. Cobra Chickens is a slang term for Canada Geese that gained popularity in 2018 after a post on Twitter went viral from a farm worker. Consider yourself lucky if you've never been chased by a cobra chicken!
COINS: Canada has some iconic coins, including the $1 loonie and the $2 toonie. DYK: In 2017, the Canadian Mint ran a contest and Canadians chose "Churchill" as the toonie polar bear's official name, a reference both to Winston Churchill and to the common polar bear sightings in Churchill, Manitoba. Canada has even commemorated the coins with monuments: the "Big Loonie" in Echo Bay, Ontario and the "Giant Toonie" in Campbellford, Ontario.
COOKS: Celebrity Cooks was one of Canada’s first cooking shows, airing from 1975 to 1987 and hosted by Bruno Gerussi of The Beachcombers fame. It mixed celebrity guests with easy, tasty recipes, inspiring a generation of home cooks. Since then, Canadian chefs have kept the country’s culinary scene vibrant, from Stephen Yan of the Canadian-produced Wok with Yan to Chuck Hughes, Lynn Crawford, Mark McEwan, Matty Matheson, Michael Smith, Anna Olson, Susur Lee, and Rob Feenie. These chefs showcase Canada’s diverse culinary talent on TV, in restaurants, and in cookbooks.
CRABS: Canada is the largest producer of snow crab in the world, accounting for about two-thirds of the global supply! The provinces of Newfoundland and Quebec provide Canada and the world with hundreds of tonnes of snow crab each year. Snow crabs have white flesh with a tinge of pink and a slightly salty flavour offering the perfect balance of sweet and briny.
CRAVE: Crave is a popular Canadian streaming service offering a wide range of content and programming. Launched by Bell Media in 2014, Crave provides Canadians with access to a rich library of movies, TV shows, and original content. It has become a go-to platform for Canadian viewers craving top-quality entertainment, including hit series like "Game of Thrones," "The Handmaid's Tale," and Canadian originals like "Letterkenny." With its extensive selection and exclusive offerings, Crave has cemented itself as a key player in the Canadian streaming landscape.
CRIED: The Girl Who Cried Pearls made history in 2026 by winning the Academy Award for Best Animated Short Film. Produced by the National Film Board of Canada, the stop-motion film was created by Montréal-based directors Chris Lavis and Maciek Szczerbowski, and is set in early 20th-century Montréal. Featuring Canadian voice actor Colm Feore, it’s a powerful example of homegrown storytelling earning global recognition.
CRIER: Before newspapers or social media, Canadian towns relied on the town crier to spread the news. Ringing a bell and shouting “Hear Ye! Hear Ye!”, they announced royal proclamations, local events, and important updates. Today, town criers are a cherished part of Canada’s history, keeping this lively tradition alive at festivals and ceremonies!
CURSE: The Oak Island mystery is a series of stories and legends concerning buried treasure and unexplained objects found on or near Oak Island in Nova Scotia. Since the 18th century, attempts have been made to find treasure and artifacts. Hypotheses about artifacts present on the island range from pirate treasure to Shakespearean manuscripts to the Holy Grail or the Ark of the Covenant. A "curse" on the treasure is said to have originated more than a century ago and states that seven men will die in the search for the treasure before it is found. This intriguing tale has been the subject of the popular TV series "The Curse of Oak Island," which follows brothers Rick and Marty Lagina as they explore the island's mysteries.
CURVE: Morant's Curve is a scenic viewpoint near Lake Louise of a dramatic bend along the Bow River where trains pass through the Canadian Rockies. It's a popular viewpoint for photographers in Banff National Park. The iconic Canadian shot that most photographers are looking for is of a beautiful, crimson red train making its way towards the camera through the landscape. The location was named after photographer Nicholas Morant, who was working for the Canadian Pacific Railway in the mid 20th century.
DAISY: Happy Mother's Day from Canuckle! The daisy is a symbol of love, purity, and new beginnings – just like the care and strength of a mother. In Canada, the daisy is known for its simple beauty, blooming across meadows and fields from coast to coast. Whether you're gifting flowers or simply enjoying a peaceful moment in nature, today's the perfect day to appreciate all the moms in your life!
DANCE: Canada is a country rich in multicultural heritage and culture, part of which is dance. Long before we called this land Canada, Aboriginal dancers were practising dance. Powwow dances are beautiful expressions of Indigenous spirituality, history and culture. When more people began immigrating to Canada in the 1900s, they brought with them bits of rich heritage and culture from all over the globe. This influx of international talent is what led to the creation of most of our dance institutions today, including the National Ballet of Canada and the Royal Winnipeg Ballet, Canada's oldest ballet company and the longest continuously operating ballet company in North America. Sikh-Canadian Gurdeep Pandher of the Yukon, has been spreading joy, hope and positivity across Canada with his Bhangra dancing - a traditional folk dance of Punjab. Check out www.gurdeep.ca and get ready to dance!
DIVER: Canada has produced some talented divers over the years who have had incredible success on the world stage. Jennifer Abel from Montreal, Quebec has two Olympic medals for Canada, and her ten medals (six silver, four bronze) are a record for most medals by a Canadian in diving at the world championships. Montreal diver Émilie Heymans was the first Canadian to win medals in four consecutive Olympics. Alexandre Despatie, also from Montreal, is the most decorated male diver in Canadian history, winning two Olympic silver medals and reaching eight podiums at the world championships, including three gold medals. The 2023 World Aquatics Championships are currently taking place in Fukuoka, Japan, featuring Canadian springboard, platform and high divers.
DOCKS: Across Canada, Victoria Day weekend is widely seen as the unofficial start of summer, and docks across lakes and cottages are finally coming back to life. Millions of Canadians head to cottages or lake regions each year for the May long weekend, making it one of the busiest travel periods of the spring season. Boats return to the water, families gather along shorelines, and communities across the country kick off the season with sunshine, fresh air, and time by the lake.
DONOR: It's National Organ and Tissue Donation Awareness Week in Canada! Every year, this week is held during the last full week of April to raise awareness about the critical need for more donors across the country and encourage Canadians to register their decision and talk to their loved ones about organ donation. Register now to become an organ and tissue donor at organtissuedonation.ca!
DONUT: Canada has the most donut shops and consumes the most donuts per capita of any other country in the world - around 1 billion annually! The donut-eating capital of Canada is Lloydminster, Alberta/Saskatchewan. National Donut Day was last Friday, June 3rd - we hope you celebrated with your favourite donut! In Canada, the preferred spelling is “doughnut”, but most dictionaries list “donut” as an acceptable variant. We wanted to include it in the game since the doughnut/donut is considered by some as Canada's unofficial national sugary snack! 🍩🍁
DOZEN: Did you know egg cartons were invented by a Canadian? Egg cartons were invented in 1911 in British Columbia by Joseph Coyle after overhearing a dispute over broken eggs between a local farmer and hotel owner. Coyle was a newspaper man and part-time inventor. He designed the very first egg carton from newspaper, with cushioned slots for each egg. The next time your dozen eggs get home safely, make sure to thank Joseph Coyle!
DRAKE: The Village of Andrew, Alberta is home to the world's largest mallard duck! The statue honours the area's wetlands and mallard nesting grounds. It features a male mallard duck (also known as a drake) with a wingspan of 23 feet, weighing 1 tonne and standing seven metres tall. This drake is not quite as famous as Canadian rapper and singer, Drake, who also starred as Jimmy Brooks in the teen drama series Degrassi: The Next Generation.
DRIFT: Along Canada’s coastlines, driftwood is carried by waves, tides, and currents before washing ashore in ever-changing shapes. It has long been used in coastal Indigenous communities for practical purposes such as carving, building, and fuel, and continues to hold cultural and creative significance. Today, it is also widely used in Canadian driftwood art, where artists transform weathered pieces into sculptures, furniture, and natural décor that reflect the beauty of the shoreline.
DRUID: Modern druidry has taken root in Canada, where groups gather to celebrate the changing seasons, honour nature, and explore Celtic-inspired spiritual traditions. From coastal ceremonies in Atlantic Canada to forest gatherings in British Columbia, Canadian druids blend ancient symbolism with local landscapes, reminding us how deeply connected many Canadians feel to the land around them.
DRYER: The word dryer is forever tied to Sidney Crosby's rise to hockey greatness. Growing up in Cole Harbour, Nova Scotia, Crosby spent hours shooting pucks in the basement of his childhood home, and the family clothes dryer bore the marks of many slapshots sent its way. This makeshift training ground played a part in shaping Crosby into the NHL legend he became. In fact, the battered dryer was even featured in an exhibit at the Nova Scotia Sport Hall of Fame, a testament to the role it played in his journey. Now, as he leads Team Canada as captain in the 4 Nations Face-Off, Crosby continues to inspire the next generation of hockey stars.
DUCKS: With roughly 22 different species of duck found in Canada, the most common is the Mallard. Saskatchewan is renowned for having some of the most abundant and productive waterfowl habitat in North America. Check out Ducks Unlimited Canada and how they are working to conserve, restore and manage Canadian wetlands.
DUMMY: Canada has a rich tradition of ventriloquism, with incredible performers like Mark Crocker, known for his lovable dummy Elmer, and Cy Leonard, the first ventriloquist to appear on Canadian television. Don Bryan has been recognized as one of the world's top ventriloquists, and he is also a leading expert in the art of creating and carving ventriloquist dummies. These talented artists proved that even a "dummy" can be the star of the show!
DUNES: The world's smallest desert can be found in the Yukon! In truth, the moniker is used in good fun as the Carcross Desert isn't a desert at all. The beautiful 2.5 square kilometre patch of land is a series of sand dunes left over from a glacial lake thousands of years ago. The tiny area is kept dry year-round thanks to the surrounding mountains. In contrast, the Athabasca Sand Dunes in Saskatchewan is the largest active sand surface in Canada at 1925 km² and one of the world's most northerly major sand dunes.
EATER: The Smoke Eaters (aka Smokies) have existed as both junior and senior hockey teams in Canada since the 1920s. The senior Smoke Eaters won two Allan Cup championships, 1938 and 1962, and two Ice Hockey World Championships playing for Canada in 1939 and 1961. The senior Smokies were the last independent ice hockey club to represent Canada in international competition before the Canada men's national ice hockey team was established in 1963. The current Trail Smoke Eaters are a junior A ice hockey team from Trail, British Columbia, that are part of the British Columbia Hockey League. Learn more about the Smoke Eaters in Craig Baird's Canadian History Ehx podcast episode!
EERIE: As Halloween draws near, Canada is home to some truly eerie locations that promise spine-chilling experiences! From the haunted Fairmont Banff Springs Hotel in Alberta, known for its ghostly bride roaming the halls, to the Ottawa Jail Hostel, where visitors report unsettling encounters, the country offers numerous sites steeped in supernatural lore. These places not only showcase Canada's rich history but also the spooky tales that come alive during the Halloween season. So, if you're in the mood for some thrills this October, consider exploring one of these eerie spots!
EIGHT: Canada has a proud tradition in rowing, especially in the men's and women's eight events. The coxed eight boat class (8 rowers with one oar each and a coxswain to steer) has been Canada's most successful rowing event with notable triumphs on the world stage. The Canadian men's and women's eight teams have collectively won a total of six Olympic medals: two golds and four silvers.
EJECT: The ejection seat, invented in Britain during the 1940s by Sir James Martin of Martin-Baker Aircraft, has saved thousands of pilots’ lives. Canada was among the early adopters, equipping its jets with this life-saving technology. Today, Royal Canadian Air Force pilots flying CF-18 Hornets rely on rocket-powered ejection systems that can launch them clear of danger in under two seconds – a dramatic but vital safeguard in Canadian aviation.
ELECT: Canada is a representative democracy. During an election, all Canadian citizens who are at least 18 years old on election day can vote in their electoral district.
EQUAL: In 1927, five women who have since become known as the Famous Five launched a legal challenge that would mark a turning point for equality rights in Canada. Emily Murphy, Nellie McClung, Louise McKinney, Irene Parlby and Henrietta Muir Edwards were journalists, politicians, reformers and activists from Alberta who advocated for equal rights for women in Canada. There are statues of the Famous Five in both Ottawa and Calgary celebrating the decision of the Privy Council that women are persons and could be elected to the Senate.
EXPOS: The Montreal Expos, named after the Expo 67 World's Fair, were the first Major League Baseball franchise located outside the USA, competing from 1969 until 2004. The last World's Fair held in Canada was Expo 86 in Vancouver.
FABLE: Fables of the Green Forest introduced Canadian kids in the 1980s and 1990s to woodland adventures on TVOntario (TVO). Each episode unfolded like a classic fable, with animal characters learning simple lessons about friendship, courage, and life in the forest. It remains a nostalgic example of how storytelling on TVO helped shape early childhood viewing in Canada.
FACES: Faces Magazine is Ottawa’s premier lifestyle publication, showcasing the faces behind the city's businesses, sports, and entertainment scene. Faces highlights the best of Ottawa with a uniquely Canadian flair. From restaurants to community leaders, it’s all about connecting people and celebrating what makes the capital great!
FAITH: Religion in Canada encompasses a wide range of beliefs and customs. The constitution of Canada refers to God and the monarch carries the title of Defender of the Faith, however Canada has no official church and the government is officially committed to religious pluralism. Freedom of religion in Canada is a constitutionally protected right, allowing individuals to assemble and worship without limitation or interference.
FAUNA: Canada's fauna is as diverse as its landscapes, from majestic moose roaming the forests and playful otters frolicking in rivers, to bison grazing the plains and beavers diligently building their dams. With over 200 species of mammals, 400 species of birds, and countless other creatures, Canada is a wildlife lover's dream. Whether you're spotting a moose on a forest trail or hearing the call of a loon across a lake, Canada's fauna never fails to leave you in awe.
FERRY: Canada is home to over 180 different ferry routes with a route presently operating in each province and the majority of the territories. Transportation through waterways has always been a crucial part of Canada’s history. From the First Nations traveling by canoes through rivers, lakes and parts of the oceans to the early explorers, there has always been an emphasis on the transportation of people by boats.
FIBRE: Fibre optic internet technology has revolutionized connectivity, and here in Canada, it's also helping bridge the digital divide! In Ottawa, the National Capital FreeNet (NCF) is making waves with its Community WiFi project, in partnership with our friends at CIRA. By leveraging fibre connections from Hiboo Networks, Ottawa-Gatineau's first municipally owned fibre optic-based telecom provider, this pilot project provides free internet access to underserved communities, supporting thousands of individuals living in Ottawa Community Housing. This initiative complements CIRA's annual Net Good Grants program which provides millions of dollars in funding to community-led projects that address digital challenges in rural, remote, and Indigenous communities across Canada.
FIELD: There are so many different types of fields in Canada: sports fields, wheat fields, oil fields, and ice fields to name a few. The Canadian Prairies are known for their open skies and vast fields of grain, but Canada is also home to the world's largest non-polar ice field in the St. Elias Mountains located in Kluane National Park and Reserve, Yukon Territory.
FILMS: The film industry in Canada has grown so much over the years that it has been referred to as Hollywood North. Toronto is the home to the Toronto International Film Festival, which is considered by many in the film industry to be second only to Cannes in terms of influence. James Cameron, born in Kapuskasing, Ontario, is the writer and director of the two highest-grossing movies of all time, Avatar (2009) and Titanic (1997). The two films have combined to gross nearly $500 million dollars. Save the date: April 19, 2023 is National Canadian Film Day!
FINCH: The Fleet Finch is a two-seat, tandem training biplane produced by Fleet Aircraft of Fort Erie, Ontario. Over several years beginning in 1939, a total of 447 Finches were built. The Finch was a mainstay of the Royal Canadian Air Force prior to and during the early part of the Second World War.
FLAIR: National Ribbon Skirt Day on January 4 honours Indigenous women and the ribbon skirt – a centuries-old spiritual symbol of womanhood, identity, and resilience. The skirt represents a deep connection to Mother Earth, culture, and the passing of knowledge across generations. With their flowing designs and vibrant ribbons, these garments embody both tradition and flair, inviting all Canadians to learn, reflect, and celebrate the richness of Indigenous cultures. The day was inspired by the experience of Isabella Kulak, an Indigenous girl in Saskatchewan who was shamed for wearing a ribbon skirt to school.
FLASH: Today is National Lighthouse Day! Canada is home to more than 750 lighthouses, and every lighthouse emits a distinctive series of flashes known as its "characteristic." These flash sequences allow ship captains to time intervals between flashes so that they can identify lighthouses, using a publication called the List of Lights.
FLEET: The Royal Canadian Navy's (RCN) fleet is made up of numerous classes of ships, submarines and other support vessels, as well as specialized units that allow Canada to maintain one of the most active blue-water navies in the world. The Royal Canadian Air Force (RCAF) aircraft fleet ranges from huge transport aircraft to helicopters to fighters to patrol aircraft and more. They are used to carry out a multitude of roles at home and abroad, in peace and in conflict, all in support of the RCAF's mission of providing relevant, responsive and effective air power to meet the defence challenges of today and into the future. November 5 to 11 is Veterans' Week, an opportunity for Canadians to honour the extraordinary efforts and sacrifices of our veterans. Thank you for your service!
FLEUR: Today is Saint-Jean-Baptiste Day! A national holiday in the Canadian province of Quebec and celebrated by French Canadians across the country and around the world! The fleur-de-lis (also spelled fleur-de-lys) is featured on the flag of Quebec, known as the "Fleurdelisé". The white cross on a blue field recalls an ancient French military banner, and the four fleurs-de-lis are symbolic of France. In Canada, over 10 million people speak French!
FLOAT: Did you know that Canada has its own version of the Dead Sea? The waters of Little Manitou Lake near Saskatoon are roughly five times saltier than the ocean - and approximately half as salty as the Dead Sea in Israel and Jordan. Fed by underground springs, the lake is so high in sodium, magnesium and potassium salts that swimmers are able to lie back and float with zero effort whatsoever.
FLOCK: Canada is home to an incredible variety of bird species, with many of them forming large flocks during migration seasons. One fascinating example is the snow goose, which gathers in massive flocks during its annual migration from the Arctic to warmer southern regions. These flocks can contain thousands, and sometimes even tens of thousands of birds, creating breathtaking spectacles in the sky as they travel across Canada's landscapes.
FLOOR: Samuel Perry Jacks, more commonly known as "Sam Jacks", was a Canadian soldier in World War II, inventor, military and civic recreation director, sports coach, and creator of the Canadian sport of ringette. In 1936, Jacks created the game of floor hockey, and developed the first set of rules, and was recognized by the Youth Branch of the United Nations for the creation of the game.
FLYER: When it made its debut at the 1953 Canadian National Exhibition in Toronto, The Flyer roller coaster was the highest and fastest in the world at the time. Its tallest point was 19 m or 62 ft, and it could reach speeds up to 104 km or 65 miles per hour. Two four-car trains sped along the ride's 796 m or 2,612 ft long track for a total of 32 riders per train.
FOOLS: Happy April Fools' Day! A Company of Fools has been delighting audiences all across Canada since 1990 as Ottawa’s original professional Shakespeare company. They bring 90-minute versions of Shakespeare’s hits to over 35 community parks during July and August. Their shows pair Shakespeare’s text with physical theatre techniques of slap-stick, mask, and puppetry that are fun for all!
FORGE: Hamilton Forge FC is a Canadian professional soccer club based in Hamilton, Ontario, that competes in the Canadian Premier League, the top tier of Canadian soccer. Forge FC joined the CPL in 2019 as one of the league's seven inaugural teams. The team name represents Hamilton's industrious roots and aligns with its nickname "Steeltown."
FORUM: 27 years ago on March 11, 1996, the Montreal Canadiens played their last game at the Forum, a venue that had been home ice for the storied hockey team for 71 years. Forever considered as the temple of hockey, the Montreal Forum served as home for the Habs for 22 of their NHL-record 24 Stanley Cup victories, and 12 times they lifted the Cup on Forum ice.
FRESH: Happy New Year from Canuckle! Canada holds 20% of the world's freshwater supply and 9% of the world's renewable freshwater resources, but this time of year people are more excited about all of the fresh powder on ski runs across the country. It's a fresh start for 2023 - cheers to the New Year!
FULLY: The Tragically Hip, often referred to simply as the Hip, were a Canadian rock band formed in Kingston, Ontario in 1984, consisting of vocalist Gord Downie, guitarist Paul Langlois, guitarist Rob Baker, bassist Gord Sinclair, and drummer Johnny Fay. They have received numerous Canadian music awards, including 17 Juno Awards. Their album "Fully Completely" is widely considered the Hip's breakthrough record, and songs like "Wheat Kings" and "Courage" became Canadian anthems. The Hip played their final concert together in Kingston on August 20, 2016. Frontman Gord Downie passed away on October 17, 2017 after a battle with brain cancer.
GATES: The Queen's Gates is the formal entrance to Parliament Hill in Ottawa, Ontario. The Princes' Gates is a triumphal arch and a monumental gateway at Exhibition Place in Toronto, Ontario. Canada Gate was installed in London, England in the early years of the 20th century as part of the memorial to Queen Victoria. The gates were a gift from Canada, celebrating its contribution to the then British Empire.
GAUGE: In Canada, we go big - even when it comes to measuring the wind! In Lethbridge, Alberta, you'll find the world's largest wind gauge, a unique roadside attraction that stands over 17 feet tall. Lethbridge is famous for its strong Chinook winds, so the towering gauge is a fitting tribute to the city's windy reputation. Next time you’re in southern Alberta, check out this quirky Canadian landmark and see if you can "gauge" just how gusty it is!
GENIE: The Genie Awards were given out annually by the Academy of Canadian Cinema and Television to recognize the best of Canadian cinema from 1980–2012. The Genie Awards succeeded the Canadian Film Awards (1949-1978), and were merged with the Gemini Awards in 2013 to form the Canadian Screen Awards. The 11th annual Canadian Screen Awards were held at Meridian Hall in Toronto from April 11-14 to honour achievements in Canadian film, television and digital media production. Highlights of the awards ceremony air on CBC and CBC Gem tonight on the final day of Canadian Screen Week 2023!
GENRE: The Juno Awards celebrate the diversity of Canadian music across multiple genres, from pop and rock to country, hip-hop, jazz, and beyond! Since their inception in 1970, the Junos have evolved to reflect Canada's rich musical landscape, adding new genre categories over the years to spotlight emerging talent. Whether it's indie, electronic, or traditional Indigenous music, the Junos showcase the best of Canada's sound! Tonight, the Junos return to Vancouver, British Columbia, marking the city's fifth time hosting Canada's biggest night in music!
GIANT: The Sibley Peninsula just outside of Thunder Bay, Ontario is home to The Sleeping Giant, a series of cliffs which resemble a giant lying on its back. The formation is part of Sleeping Giant Provincial Park and it was voted number one on a list of The Seven Wonders of Canada, and 2007 competition sponsored by CBC. Another famous Canadian giant was "The Friendly Giant", a children's television program that aired on CBC from 1958-1985 with over 3,000 episodes!
GIFTS: Gifts are at the heart of Canada’s holiday traditions, adding warmth to long winter nights. From Secret Santas and office swaps to treats shared with neighbours, the season is all about generosity and connection. In many Indigenous cultures, gifting is rooted in reciprocity and respect, reminding us how giving strengthens community. Whether it’s a cozy toque, butter tarts, or a maple-themed surprise, the spirit of sharing shines across Canada every December.
GINGER: Did you know ginger beef is a Canadian invention? This crispy, sweet-and-spicy dish was created in the 1970s by Chef George Wong at the Silver Inn Restaurant in Calgary, Alberta. Wong’s recipe quickly won over diners and spread from Alberta to the rest of the country, becoming a staple on Chinese restaurant menus nationwide. Today, ginger beef is a delicious example of how Canadian cuisine blends global influences with local flair.
GIVER: The slang word give'r is used in Canada to mean to give it all you've got or to try as hard as possible at something. Also, today is the International Day of Charity! The day was chosen to commemorate the anniversary of the passing away of Mother Teresa of Calcutta, who received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979 for her humanitarian work. Canadians are known to be a very generous bunch of givers. In 2021, Canadians gave over $11.8 billion to charitable organizations. Consider donating to your favourite charity today, and just give'r!
GLAZE: Pottery has been produced by Europeans in Canada since the mid-17th century (and by the Indigenous peoples long before). Glaze is used to give the pottery a glassy coating, for decoration, and to preserve the pottery over time. Today is National Donut Day! To celebrate, Tim Hortons brought back two classic glazed donuts - the Walnut Crunch and the Cherry Stick! We hope you celebrate today with your favourite donut! Our favourite is the Canadian Maple! 🍩🍁
GLORY: Glory is what Canadians chase every four years at the Winter Olympics, where unforgettable moments unite the country in celebration. At Vancouver 2010, Canada won 14 gold medals, setting the record for the most golds ever by a host nation. Team Canada continues to shine, chasing sporting glory on the world stage at the 2026 Milano Cortina Games!
GOLDEN: Canada’s newest team in the Professional Women’s Hockey League is ready to shine on the West Coast – introducing the Vancouver Goldeneyes! Their name is inspired by the goldeneye duck, a hardy Pacific Northwest native known for its speed and sharp vision. The Goldeneyes bring a new burst of energy to Canada’s women’s hockey scene, and Vancouver fans can’t wait to cheer on their “golden” crew as they take flight in the PWHL.
GRACE: Merry Christmas from Canuckle! Grace is often part of Canadian holiday traditions, as many families pause on Christmas Day to say a blessing before a meal. Whether it’s a few words of thanks around the table or a quiet reflection on the year, taking a moment for grace reminds Canadians of the importance of gratitude, togetherness, and the little joys that make the season bright.
GRADE: September in Canada means back to school! Students head into a new grade, ready for fresh notebooks, sharpened pencils, and new adventures in learning. Grades mark more than just progress – they’re milestones filled with growth, challenges, and proud moments. In Quebec, high school finishes at Grade 11, after which students move on to CEGEP to continue their studies. No matter where they are in the country, every grade is a step forward in the journey of learning.
GRAFT: In the Okanagan Valley, renowned for its orchards and vineyards, grafting is a vital horticultural technique. Scion grafting involves joining a young shoot (the scion) from a prized fruit tree onto the rootstock of another, combining strengths to grow healthier, more productive plants. This method helps Okanagan growers cultivate delicious apples, cherries, and grapes suited to the region’s unique climate, supporting one of Canada’s most important fruit-growing areas.
GRAIL: For hockey fans across Canada, the Stanley Cup is often referred to as the 'Holy Grail' of hockey. The Stanley Cup, awarded annually to the champion of the National Hockey League (NHL), holds a special place in Canadian sports culture as the ultimate prize in professional hockey. With its rich history dating back to 1893, the Stanley Cup has become one of the most iconic trophies in sports, symbolizing excellence, perseverance, and the pursuit of victory. The Edmonton Oilers are the only Canadian team left with a chance to hoist hockey's holy grail this year, and they are truly Canada's team with 16 Canadian-born players in their 20-man lineup.
GRAMS: When Canada switched to the metric system in the 1970s, grams replaced ounces as the standard way to measure small weights. Today, you’ll spot grams on everything from nutrition labels to coffee bags – a daily reminder of Canada’s move toward metric and its blend of precision and practicality!
GRANT: The Government of Canada offers funding through grants and contribution (Gs&Cs) programs that help support a variety of jobs, research, training and financial assistance across the country. A grant can provide funding to individuals, nonprofits, community organizations and small businesses to support upcoming projects, programs and initiatives. For many Canadians, the ability to access, stay safe and succeed on the internet is still out of reach. To help close this gap, CIRA is launching its 2024 grants program to support not-for-profits, Indigenous communities, researchers and registered charities across the country that are working to bridge that digital divide. Learn more about CIRA's Net Good Grants program!
GRAVE: Happy Halloween from Canuckle! 🎃 Halloween is the perfect time to explore some of Canada's most haunted grave sites. One eerie spot is Fairview Lawn Cemetery in Halifax, where victims of the Titanic disaster were laid to rest. Many visitors report strange occurrences near the graves, with whispers of spirits lingering on the grounds. Another spooky destination is Victoria’s Ross Bay Cemetery in British Columbia, where tales of ghostly apparitions wandering among the graves keep visitors on edge. Canada's haunted history runs deep, and during the Halloween season, these grave sites become even more chilling!
GRAZE: Canada is home to over 800,000 sheep, grazing across pastures in provinces like Ontario, Alberta, and Quebec - together accounting for over 70% of the national flock. These flocks support sustainable farming, help maintain healthy grasslands, and are an important part of Canada’s agricultural heritage. Today, there are about 8,400 sheep farms across the country.
GREAT: Although it is unknown who coined the term “Great White North” in reference to Canada, the nickname has been in use for many decades. “Great” because it’s the second largest country in the world. “White” because of the amount of Arctic frozen tundra and snow within the country. Finally, “North” because not only does Canada take up most of the northern half of North America, it also stretches nearly to the North Pole! Canada is also home to the Great Lakes, the largest group of freshwater lakes on Earth, as well as Great Bear Lake and Great Slave Lake in the Northwest Territories.
GREBE: The grebe is a type of water bird commonly found in Canada, especially in wetlands and lakes. Known for their striking appearance and elaborate mating dances, grebes are expert swimmers and divers. Some species, like the Western Grebe, even perform synchronized "rushing" displays, where they dash across the water's surface together in a spectacular show of coordination!
GRILL: Happy Father's Day from Canuckle! Every year, on the third Sunday in June, families across the country fire up their grills to honour dads with a feast of barbecued delights. From juicy steaks and burgers to fresh fish and vegetables, the grill becomes the centerpiece of many Canadian Father's Day celebrations. It's a time for family gatherings, backyard fun, and enjoying the great outdoors. Whether it's a classic barbecue or a gourmet grilling experience, Father's Day in Canada is a perfect occasion to fire up the grill and enjoy some quality time with loved ones.
GULLS: Along Canada’s coastlines, lakeshores, and even city skylines, gulls are a familiar sight. These adaptable seabirds can be found from the Atlantic to the Pacific and across the Great Lakes, often thriving wherever water and people meet. Known for their bold behaviour and opportunistic feeding habits, gulls have become one of the most recognizable birds in Canadian landscapes year-round.
HAPPY: Happy New Year from Canuckle! According to the 2023 World Happiness Report that was released on the International Day of Happiness, Canada ranks as the 13th happiest country in the world among the 137 countries included in the report. Scandinavian countries continue to hold the top spots in the rankings, with Finland in first place for the sixth year in a row.
HELIX: Helix is a Canadian hard rock and heavy metal band from Kitchener, Ontario. They formed in 1974, and are best known for their 1984 single "Rock You". Helix have toured with bands such as Kiss, Aerosmith, Rush, Mötley Crüe, Alice Cooper, Whitesnake, Heart, and Motörhead among others.
HIKER: November 17th is National Take A Hike Day! A day that encourages us to get out there and hit the trails, explore the great outdoors, and embrace the beauty of nature. Canada is a hiker's paradise, with kilometres and kilometres of beautiful coastal walks and woodland trails like no other place in the world. The Trans Canada Trail is Canada’s national trail and is the longest network of multi-use recreational trails in the world!
HOMES: The word HOMES is a handy mnemonic many Canadians use to remember the names of the Great Lakes: Huron, Ontario, Michigan, Erie, and Superior. Together, these five vast freshwater lakes hold about 21% of the world’s surface fresh water and border both Canada and the United States. From boating and fishing to providing drinking water, the Great Lakes are an essential part of life and nature in Canada.
HOSTS: Canada has been the birthplace of many beloved television hosts who have entertained audiences both nationally and internationally. One notable example is Alex Trebek, best known for hosting the iconic game show 'Jeopardy!' for over three decades. Other famous Canadian hosts include Howie Mandel, Monty Hall, Rick Mercer, George Stromboulopoulos, Ron MacLean, Gerry Dee, Jillian Harris, Jesse Palmer, Jessi Cruickshank, Jon Montgomery, Marilyn Denis, Ben Mulroney, Dini Petty, Bryan Baeumler, and Drew and Jonathan Scott. So, whether it's game shows, talk shows, or variety shows, Canada has been home to some of the most memorable hosts in television history!
HUSKY: The Canadian Inuit Dog, commonly known as the Canadian Husky or Qimmiq, is a working sled dog breed that has been used for centuries by Indigenous peoples in the Arctic. Sled dogs are also used for recreational purposes and racing events, such as the Iditarod Trail and the Yukon Quest. Dog sledding, or "mushing," is a popular and unique way to experience the winter wonderland in Canada. What better way to explore the vast, snow-covered landscape of Canada than with a team of energetic huskies leading the way!
HYDRO: Waterpower is Canada's most abundant source of clean and renewable electricity, providing more than 60% of Canada's total electricity today. Canada is the fourth largest generator of hydroelectricity in the world.
IDIOM: An idiom is a phrase whose meaning isn’t obvious from the words themselves. Canada has plenty of its own: you might hear someone say “Give’r” to mean “go for it,” “double-double” for a coffee with two creams and two sugars, “snowbirds” for Canadians who head south in the winter, or the classic “Eh?” at the end of a sentence to check for agreement. These colourful expressions show how Canadians have turned everyday language into something uniquely their own, full of humour, culture, and local flavour.
INDIE: Canada's indie scene is bursting with creativity! From homegrown musicians and filmmakers to independent game developers, Canadians are making waves with original, outside-the-box ideas. Whether it's a soulful song, a thought-provoking documentary, or a beautifully crafted game, Canada's indie creators prove that with passion and persistence, you don't need a blockbuster budget to make a big impact. The Great White North is full of independent spirit!
ISLET: Today is World Diabetes Day! Celebrated annually on November 14th, the day marks the birthday of Canadian medical scientist Frederick Banting who, along with Charles Best, first conceived the idea which led to the discovery of insulin in 1922. Insulin is a peptide hormone produced by beta cells of the pancreatic islets. It regulates the metabolism of carbohydrates, fats and protein by promoting the absorption of glucose from the blood into liver, fat and skeletal muscle cells.
IVORY: International Inuit Day on November 7 celebrates the rich cultural heritage of Inuit communities across Canada's Arctic, including their incredible craftsmanship. Among their many innovations, Inuit carvers have long used natural materials like ivory to craft intricate art pieces and practical tools. Traditional Inuit snow goggles (Inuktitut: ilgaak or iggaak), often made from ivory or bone, were designed with narrow slits to protect against the bright Arctic sun reflecting off the snow - an innovative design to prevent snow blindness.
JELLY: The colourful rows of houses in downtown St. John's are often referred to as Jelly Bean Row. The vibrantly coloured Victorian row houses help give the city its distinctive character. According to folklore, the houses got their distinctive colours so returning fishermen could easily find their houses at night through the thick fog.
JETTY: In Canada, jetties are a common sight along the coastlines, providing protection for harbours and enhancing the beauty of waterfront areas. One notable example is the Chambly Jetty in Quebec, which stretches into the Richelieu River. This historic jetty was originally built to help guide boats and protect the harbour from strong currents. Today, it's a popular spot for locals and visitors alike, offering scenic views and a glimpse into Canada's maritime heritage.
JEWEL: Looking for the biggest jewel in Canada? The town of Black Diamond, Alberta, is home to the world's largest black diamond! This striking monument was unveiled during the town's centennial Jubilee in 2007, paying homage to its namesake and rich coal mining history. Standing 1.22 metres wide and crafted from painted aluminum, the diamond is more than just a dazzling sight - it symbolizes the resilience and ingenuity of the community that once thrived on coal mining. On January 1, 2023, Black Diamond took on a new chapter in its history by amalgamating with its neighbour, Turner Valley, to form the town of Diamond Valley. Today, Diamond Valley is celebrated not only for its jewel, but also for its vibrant arts scene and stunning foothills views, making it a true gem of Alberta!
JUDGE: The Supreme Court of Canada consists of nine judges, including the Chief Justice of Canada, who are appointed by the Governor in Council. The current Chief Justice is Richard Wagner, who succeeded the longest-serving Chief Justice in Canadian history and the first woman to hold the position - Beverley McLachlin.
JUICE: Canada is a nation that loves its juice – from classic apple and orange varieties to tart cranberry and sweet grape juice. Canadian farmers produce millions of litres of fruit juice each year, and juice has long been a staple at breakfasts, school lunches, and summer picnics across the country. Whether freshly pressed or store-bought, it’s a tasty reminder of Canada’s rich fruit-growing regions.
JUMBO: Jumbo Video is a Canadian brand of franchised video stores that operated in Canada until 2018. The company was founded in May, 1987 and at one point claimed to be the third-largest player in the Canadian video rental industry. It was well known for offering free popcorn to customers, regardless of whether they rented videos. There is actually one remaining Jumbo Video Microplay store still open in London, Ontario. Check it out for the nostalgia and stay for the popcorn!
JUMPS: In Canada, trampolining isn't just a hobby – it's a celebrated sport that takes leaps and bounds to new heights! Canadian athletes have excelled in this dynamic sport, with trampoline gymnastics becoming an Olympic event in 2000. Canadian trampoline gymnast Rosie MacLennan won back-to-back gold medals in 2012 and 2016, making her the only trampolinist to defend her Olympic title successfully.
KARMA: Karma is the idea that what you put into the world comes back to you – a philosophy that inspired Farming Karma, a family-run Canadian beverage company based in Kelowna, British Columbia. Founded by Karma and Kuku Gill, longtime Okanagan orchardists, the brand grew out of decades of BC fruit farming and a desire to turn homegrown apples and cherries into better-for-you sodas. Today, Farming Karma products are made with real fruit from the family’s orchards and enjoyed across Canada, carrying a simple message at its core: good fruit, good people, and good karma.
KINGS: Today is Commonwealth Day! The 56 member countries of the Commonwealth, including Canada, celebrate Commonwealth Day every year on the second Monday in March. It is a day of observance by more than 2 billion citizens of their common bonds and the contribution of the Commonwealth to the creation of a harmonious global environment. Canada has been a monarchy for centuries - first under the kings of France in the 16th, 17th and 18th centuries, then under the British Crown in the 18th and 19th centuries, and now as a kingdom in her own right.
KNIFE: The city of Yellowknife is the capital of the Northwest Territories and the territory's only city. The city gets its name from the copper tools historically made and traded by the local Dene First Nation. The city and Yellowknife Bay were named after the Yellowknives, a Dene band who lived on the islands of Great Slave's East Arm and travelled as far north as the Arctic coast to obtain copper for knives and other implements. They, in turn, acquired their name from the copper-bladed knives they carried.
LANCE: One of the most prominent symbols of Canada is the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) "Mountie," wearing their red serge uniform and brown Stetson. Put many of these Mounties on black horses, have them perform intricate formations in front of a crowd, and you have another of Canada's most recognizable icons: the RCMP Musical Ride. The riders carry lances, while the Officer in Charge carries a sword. "The Charge" is one of the final and the most powerful manoeuvres performed by the RCMP Musical Ride. The finely trained horses are lined up and held in position by their riders until the rider lowers the lance and bellows "Charge!" and the horses and riders thunder forward in battle cry of times past.
LARGE: With a landmass of almost 10 million square kilometres, Canada is the second-largest country in the world.
LASER: Canadians Bruce Kirby and Ian Bruce invented the iconic Laser sailboat. The Laser became one of the world's most popular racing sailboats. It became so popular that the Olympic committee added the Laser as an Olympic-class boat for men in 1996 and women in 2008. The Laser’s enduring popularity, though, comes from the thousands of recreational sailors who experience the pure pleasure of single-handing a Laser on a breezy day.
LAUGH: Just for Laughs is a comedy festival held each July in Montreal, Quebec, Canada. Founded in 1983 at the Saint-Denis Theatre, it has grown to become the largest international comedy festival in the world. Hundreds of big-name comedians have participated, including Jim Carrey, Trevor Noah, Joan Rivers, Jimmy Fallon, Kevin Hart, and Amy Schumer. It's Canada History Week! This year it takes place from November 21 to 27 and the theme is "Arts, Culture, and Creators". The week encourages Canadians to reflect upon and engage with Canada's past, and serves as an opportunity for Canadian citizens to learn more about the people, places, and events that shaped the country they know today. Canuckle will be featuring words all week that tie in with the theme! #HistoryWeek2022
LAYER: Nanaimo Bars are a Canadian dessert staple originating in Nanaimo, a city on Vancouver Island in British Columbia. It consists of three layers: a graham wafer crumb and shredded coconut base, a custard-flavoured butter icing filling, and a chocolate ganache topping. The Nanaimo bar was popularized nationwide after being highlighted as a classic Canadian dessert at Expo 86. In 2006, the Nanaimo bar was declared Canada’s favourite confection by a reader’s poll in the National Post.
LEDGE: Balancing Rock in Nova Scotia is a famous volcanic rock balanced precariously on a ledge above the waves of St. Mary's Bay. Called "Nature's Time Post", the Balancing Rock is a narrow vertical column of basalt, balanced on its tip that appears to defy gravity. It is estimated to weigh over 20 tonnes and stands 9 metres (20 feet) tall. It's the most photographed of Long Island's striking basalt formations.
LEGAL: Street Legal is a Canadian legal drama television series, which aired on CBC Television from 1987 to 1994. Street Legal was the longest-running one-hour scripted drama in the history of Canadian television, holding the record for twenty years before being surpassed by Heartland in 2015.
LEMON: One of the greatest mysteries of the Canadian Rockies is the legend of the so-called “Lost Lemon Mine.” The Lost Lemon Mine is a legendary gold deposit reputedly somewhere between the Crowsnest Pass and the Highwood River in southwestern Alberta, discovered about 1870 by prospectors Frank Lemon and "Blackjack." Thousands have since searched for the fabulous lode; many have died mysteriously. Check out Craig Baird's Canadian History Ehx podcast to learn more!
LEVEE: Happy New Year from Canuckle! In Canada, the word "levee" has a unique historical and cultural significance! Originating from the French word "lever," meaning "to rise," a levee is a New Year's Day reception traditionally hosted by the Governor General, Lieutenant Governors, military establishments, and municipalities. This custom dates back to the 17th century, introduced by French colonial governors. Today, it is a cherished Canadian tradition where citizens gather to exchange New Year's greetings, enjoy refreshments, and celebrate community spirit.
LEVEL: The High Level Bridge in Lethbridge, Alberta is the longest, highest trestle bridge in the world. It is 1.6 km long and is 96 metres high and was completed in 1909. This Canadian Pacific Railway rail line has stood the test of time and is still used today with numerous trains crossing the bridge throughout the day.
LIGHT: With the world's longest coastline and more than half the earth's area covered in lakes, Canada is home to more than 750 lighthouses. Lighthouses across Canada have long symbolized strength, safety and safe harbour. The first lighthouse in Canada was built in Louisbourg on Cape Breton Island, Nova Scotia, in 1734. Did you know that every lighthouse has a distinctive flash pattern?
LINES: Canadian engineer John D. Millar devised what now seems a straightforward manner of helping drivers to share the road - painting lines to divide lanes and to separate traffic moving in opposite directions. Millar was working for the Ontario Department of Transport when he came up with the idea in 1930. A stretch of highway between Quebec and Ontario was the first to receive the treatment.
